verse_quote: the second year of Darius the king . . . sixth month ... first day.
note:
Each of Haggai’s sermons is carefully dated, which is an uncommon feature among the biblical prophets. These dates connect the events described in the book with the wider backdrop of world history. This oracle occurred probably on August 29, 520 B.C., when stability was returning to the empire after a time of unrest following Darius’s accession. The sixth month was the time for harvesting the fruit trees, after harvesting the other crops, so it was a natural time to assess the success of the agricultural year. The first day of the month, the “new moon,” was a festival day, when crowds would likely have gathered at the site of the temple. Haggai’s message was addressed publicly to the leaders so that the people could respond as well (1:12).

**Zerubbabel.** He may be the same person as Sheshbazzar (cf. Ezra 1:8), since both are said to have rebuilt the temple. Sheshbazzar could be an official Persian name. However, it is perhaps more likely that they were separate individuals. Zerubbabel was the grandson of King Jehoiachin (1 Chr. 3:19) and a descendant of David (2:23 note), appointed by the Persians as the governor of the province of Yehud (Judah).

**Joshua the son of Jehozadak.** See 1 Chr. 6:15. A descendant of Zadok the priest. Under Persian rule, Zerubbabel had responsibility over the daily civil affairs of the region. As high priest, Joshua dealt with religious matters.

An expression of implied displeasure (2:14). Verses 2–11 indict the spiritual indifference and misplaced priorities of God’s people.

**the time has not yet come.** Their objection is not to the rebuilding itself, but to the timing of it. The objections may be seasonal, since it is harvesttime when Haggai is ministering, or more generally economic, because their land is in trouble (cf. vv. 10, 11). The Persian army is making preparations at this time for an assault on Egypt, to which the empire’s vassals, including Judah, are expected to contribute. There seems to be a general discouragement about the future. Such excuses show that they are not pursuing God’s kingdom and righteousness (cf. Matt. 6:33).

**the house of the LORD** **.** The Jerusalem temple is the dwelling place of God’s special presence with His people during the old covenant era (1 Kin. 8:27–30). Today God is graciously present in His temple, the church (1 Cor. 3:16, 17).

Haggai reveals the hypocrisy of their objections by a rhetorical question. The houses probably have elaborate wooden walls and ceilings (1 Kin. 7:3; Jer. 22:14). They are living in comparative luxury while God’s house lies in ruins. More specifically, since the word “paneled” elsewhere is usually used with reference to the temple, they apparently have precisely the resources to build their own houses that they claim are lacking to build God’s house.
The people may be blaming God for the lack of fruitfulness, but the issue is their own lack of obedience.

Their economic and social hardship is the effect of God’s covenant curse on their disobedience (Lev. 26:20; Deut. 11:8–15; 28:29, 38–40). God has frustrated their efforts because of their lack of concern for His glory. These kinds of futility curses are common in ancient Near Eastern covenant treaties.

**a bag with holes.** The people are compared to a laborer who takes the wages for which he has worked hard and deliberately puts them into a bag with holes, so that much for which he has worked is lost on the way home. As a result, their lives are frustratingly unfulfilling.

verse_quote: take pleasure in it and that I may be glorified.
note: God’s purpose in the enterprise is the special joy He will take in this edifice and the appropriate honor He will thereby receive from His people. Their lack of concern for rebuilding indicates their lack of spiritual health.
The focus of their lives is on building their own personal fortunes and families rather than building God’s kingdom.

The drought on Judah’s crops is God’s curse on their agriculture, in keeping with His covenant (1:6 note; Deut. 7:13). The Hb. word translated “ruins” in v. 9 sounds like the Hb. word for “drought” here. Haggai’s play on words reinforces the point that the drought is God’s response to their neglect of His house.

A common term used by the prophets for those of God’s people who remain faithful to Him in the midst of unbelief (Is. 10:22; cf. Zech. 13:9). Using this term here focuses attention on the fact that God has brought them through the judgment of the Babylonian exile. Paul later points to a faithful remnant in Israel—Jews who have embraced Christ (Rom. 11:5).

**voice of the LORD** **... words of Haggai.** They recognize God’s word through the voice of the prophet. God’s revelation always accomplishes its intended purpose (Is. 55:1; Heb. 4:12).

**the people feared the LORD** **.** Given the consequences for unfaithfulness that they have already received, this is a wise and appropriate response.

As the people repent of their sin, they receive the greatest assurance possible, the presence of God. God’s gracious presence with His people is the heart of the covenant relationship (Zech. 8:8 note).

God Himself brings about His people’s response by His presence with them. Haggai emphasizes the internal response by the threefold repetition of “spirit.” God’s Spirit works efficaciously through His word, which Haggai has given, in order to achieve His sovereign purpose (cf. Is. 55:11). The outworking of repentance is renewed obedience.
Probably September 21, 520 B.C., just twenty-three days after the initial oracle.

The Lord again speaks to the people, this time encouraging them to continue building. Reports about the magnificence of the now-destroyed temple of Solomon are apparently a source of discouragement (v. 3). The Lord first assures them of His continued presence with them—a promise for the present (vv. 4, 5). Second, He assures them about the future goal of their project (vv. 6–9). Though it appears humble in comparison, the glory of this temple will finally far outstrip Solomon’s temple because it will be graced by the presence of the Messiah Himself (v. 9 note).

**2:1 seventh month ... twenty-first.** October 17, 520 B.C. The year is not explicitly mentioned; presumably, it is still the second year of Darius (see 1:15). According to Lev. 23:33–43, this is the last day of the Feast of Tabernacles, during which God’s people are to rejoice in God’s provision for them in the wilderness and the blessings of the harvest. It is once again the time of a major assembly, giving the prophet an opportunity to address a large group of people. There is not much to rejoice in this year, however, since their harvest is meager (1:11). Solomon’s temple was also dedicated at the time of the same festival (1 Kin 8:2).

Haggai’s first sermon was addressed to the leaders because they had to initiate the work. The common people are included here because this message is intended to encourage them about the task at hand. Remembering the first exodus and wilderness wandering is particularly poignant for this group of people who have just recently experienced their own exodus from Babylon.

verse_quote: this house in its former glory.
note: Verses 1–3 suggest that the people are discouraged by the new temple’s relative lack of splendor (cf. 2 Chr. 3; 4) and by the difficulty of the task ahead of them. Although the rebuilt temple is similar in its dimensions to the old one, it lacks the physical splendor and the political significance of Solomon’s temple. It also lacked the spiritual glory (Hb. _kabod_) of the Lord, which departed from Solomon’s temple in the days of Ezekiel before its destruction by the Babylonians (Ezek. 10).

Threefold repetition adds emphasis to the command. Similar commands accompanied the building of Solomon’s temple (1 Chr. 22:13; 28:20; cf. Gal. 6:9) and the entering of the land under Joshua (Josh. 1:6).

**I am with you.** The Lord’s presence and His sustaining strength guarantee the ultimate success of their labors. This promise is at the heart of God’s covenant relationship with His people (Ex. 33:15, 16; cf. Heb. 13:5).

verse_quote: covenant that I made with you.
note: God’s covenant promises, made with His people in the exodus from Egypt, now assure them of His presence (cf. Ex. 33:12–17; Num. 11:16, 17). His mighty Spirit is present, just as in the days of the great deliverance from Egypt (cf. Zech. 4:6).

As is common in the Prophets, the near and distant future are telescoped, or compressed together. Here references to the glory of the second temple are juxtaposed with a picture of the final universal judgment on the cosmos. While this shaking may be prefigured by political events occurring shortly after the time of Haggai (e.g., the defeat of Persia by the Greeks), the ultimate shaking of the created order is still to come (Heb. 12:26–28). The Feast of Booths (or Tabernacles), with its reenactment of the wilderness period, always had a forward-looking focus, anticipating the greater fulfillment of God’s promises. It was an annual reminder that the earthly land of Canaan was not their real home. This longing would have been intensified during times of difficulty, such as in the days of Haggai. The language of shaking the earth is typical of theophanies, when the presence of the Lord is manifested on earth. Here the ultimate appearing of the Lord is in view.

Though the Hb. term translated “treasures” could refer to a person (i.e., the Messiah), the immediate context here favors a reference to the things desired by all nations (i.e., the things precious to them), especially since the Hb. verb is plural. Verse 8 speaks of such precious things, and the decree of King Darius, during whose reign Haggai ministered, alludes to precious things being contributed to the temple building project (Ezra 6:3–5, 8, 9). Here Haggai probably echoes Isaiah’s promise of an Israel made rich by the wealth of the nations (Is. 60:5). In other words, he speaks of the messianic age.

**fill this house with glory.** God’s intention is to honor Himself by manifesting His glorious presence before “all nations.” As God’s presence fills the temple, the nations come to the light (Is. 2:3–5; 60:3).

As the sovereign possessor of all things (cf. Pss. 24:1; 50:9–12), God will bring about both His own glorification and His people’s inheritance of the nations’ wealth (Is. 60:5). As Haggai delivers this prophecy, much of the silver and gold that was looted from the temple by Nebuchadnezzar has not yet been returned. See note on v. 7.

The tabernacle and temple are filled with God’s glory (Ex. 40:34, 35; 1 Kin. 8:10, 11), and Haggai anticipates this happening again when the temple is reconstructed. This promise of greater glory is realized in Christ, the greatest manifestation of God’s presence and glory (Mal. 3:1; John 1:14).

**in this place I will give peace.** This peace (Hb. _shalom_) means more than the absence of conflict. It implies prosperity and a sense of total well-being, nothing short of full salvation. Christ gives peace to believers now (John 14:27), but ultimate fulfillment awaits the time when the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are the temple of the New Jerusalem (Rev. 21:22).

verse_quote: twenty-fourth day of the ninth month.
note: This date has no particular significance in terms of the festival calendar, but it is the most important date in the book, being repeated three times (2:10, 18, 20). Its significance comes from the event noted in v. 18, the symbolic refounding of the temple. The sequence of time is important for interpreting the third message, which begins on a note of judgment (vv. 10–14). The people repented and began the work on September 21, 520 B.C. (1:15), and Haggai brought a message of encouragement on October 17 of the same year (2:1–9). Here, on December 18, he brings another cautionary message. It is not enough to rebuild the temple; the deeper issue of the people’s defilement before a holy God must be dealt with.

This portion of Haggai’s third sermon, emphasizing the extensive defilement of the people and their efforts, builds on an object lesson taken from the Mosaic ceremonial law. One of the primary tasks of the priests is to teach the law, answering questions about its content and meaning (cf. Deut. 33:10). The questions that the Lord tells Haggai to direct to the priests are designed to show that while ceremonial holiness is not transferable (v. 12), ceremonial defilement is (v. 13). Haggai then applies the lesson of the preceding questions to his hearers (v. 14). They have defiled the work of the temple and their offerings because their estrangement from God is deeper than they realized. The mere presence of a rebuilt temple will not render them holy as a people (cf. Jer. 7:3–7); God demands genuine change of heart and life, not mere outward conformity.
This word signals a transition from indictment to blessing, as a result of the rebuilding of the temple. In spite of their past defilement, the holy God is determined to bless them (v. 19).

This verse draws on Amos 4:9 and Deut. 28:22. Such natural disasters and lack of agricultural productivity, the bitter fruit of disobedience to the Lord’s covenant (1:6 note; Deut. 28:22), are God’s way of getting His people’s attention. Yet as in the time of Amos, these judgments have not yet brought the people to repentance.

verse_quote: Is the seed yet in the barn?
note:
The seed for the next year has already been planted but it is too soon to anticipate by normal means what the outcome will be.

**the vine, the fig tree, the pomegranate, and the olive tree.** The four main fruit trees in Israel.

**I will bless you.** God’s grace will nonetheless overcome the sin and defilement of His people. Though He chastises them, in the end mercy triumphs over judgment. This is the outworking of the Lord’s promise in v. 9.

The last of Haggai’s sermons, given the same day as the previous address (v. 10), returns to the theme of the latter-day glory of the temple (v. 6 note). Again, future events are telescoped as Haggai interweaves mention of the coming Messiah (v. 23) with references to the shaking of the cosmos and God’s final victory over the nations (vv. 21, 22). When God ultimately shakes all things, then everything will be as it should be.

The military and political powers of the nations finally submit to God’s lordship (Dan. 2:44; 7:27). The nation is left unspecified since all nations must bow to His rule. The language is saturated with traditional themes and images recalling the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah, the destruction of the Egyptian chariots in the exodus, and the conquest of the land under Joshua. God will again do the great things He has done for His people in the past.

See note on Zech. 12:3.

**my servant.** Like his ancestor David, Zerubbabel is God’s chosen representative to accomplish His work. Isaiah speaks of a greater Servant who will come, whom Zerubbabel foreshadows (Is. 42:10). Jesus is the descendant of Zerubbabel (Matt. 1:12) and also the Servant of God (Acts 4:27, 30).

**signet ring.** A symbol of authority, ownership, and power. Before the exile, Jeremiah used the term to describe the rejection of the Davidic king Jehoiachin (Jer. 22:24). Yet here the Lord reverses that earlier oracle, declaring that Zerubbabel represents a continuing future for the line of David. The Lord is not, after all, finished with that family. A new shoot will yet emerge from the stump of Jesse (Is. 11:1). No action is demanded of Zerubbabel or his hearers in response to this oracle. They are not summoned to throw off the yoke of their Persian oppressors. They are simply to wait with confident hope for the decisive saving work that the Lord will do in His appointed time. More than five hundred years later, God accomplished this final salvation through His Son, Jesus Christ, who was descended from David according to the flesh and declared the Son of God in power at His resurrection (Rom. 1:1–4).
